newsitem.title: IRAQ: Food piles up in Iraq from oil deal, no medicine.
newsitem.headline: Food piles up in Iraq from oil deal, no medicine.

text.p: Foodstuffs bought under Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations are piling up in Iraq but no medicine has arrived yet, a U.N. source said on Thursday.
He said more than 200,000 tonnes of food had reached Iraq so far, and more was on its way.
He said seven ships carrying French and Australian wheat had unloaded at Iraq's southern port of Umm Qasr since the end of March and 13 more were expected later this month.
"But no medicine is expected until the end of April or beginning of May," he added.

Iraq, under U.N. trade sanctions since invading Kuwait in 1990, began exporting oil last December under a so-called oil-for-food deal allowing it to sell $2 billion worth of crude over six months to import mainly food and medicine.
The first shipments of food imported under the deal based on U.N. Security Council resolution 986 reached Iraq last month.

The source, who refused to be named, said the U.N. sanctions committee had so far approved more than 90 contracts for Iraqi imports under the deal, including more than 40 for the purchase of medicine and medical supplies.
The source would not say why it was taking medical supplies so long to reach Iraq.
He said more than 90 per cent of shipments were reaching Iraq via its southern port of Umm Qasr. "Umm Qasr has become the main conduit of humanitarian goods under 986," he said.

The source said a ship carrying more than 50,000 tonnes of French wheat was due in the Jordanian port of Aqaba this month. Some 1,400 tonnes of infant formula from Tunisia and 500 tonnes from France were expected via the same route.
Also from Jordan Iraq has received 1500 tonnes of iodized salt, 500 tonnes of detergent and about 250 tonnes of soap.
From Turkey Iraq has received more than 3,000 tonnes of chick peas and white beans as well as 5,000 tonnes of vegetable oil.
Late last month the Iraqi government began distributing the first food rations from the oil sales to alleviate the impact of sanctions on the Iraqi people.

The whole operation is being carried out under strict U.N. supervision. More than 120 international observers supervise the arrival, storage and distribution of food. Some 32 indepenent monitors from the Lloyds of London inspect the shipments as they enter the country.

"A few weeks ago many people told me it (986) will never start...Today our observers are mobile in the country and have undertaken 45 missions in three weeks with no one having a single problem," Iraq's U.N. coordinator Steffan de Mistura said in a news conference this week.

Iraq's revenue from the partial oil sales after setting aside 30 per cent for Gulf War reparations and other U.N. costs will be about $1.3 billion, of which $870 million has been earmarked for food and $210 million for medicine. The rest will go for education and electricity repairs.
Goods worth $260 million have to be allocated to the three Kurdish provinces in the north currently outside the control of the central government in Baghdad.
